question:
Patient note:
A 62-year-old man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed by metformin, non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with a last documented ejection fraction of 35 %, and chronic atrial fibrillation anticoagulated with apixaban was discovered by his spouse at 07:18 lying supine at the base of a ten-step wooden staircase in their split-level home; she reports hearing a loud thud but did not witness the event and denies any preceding complaint of chest pain, dyspnea, or dizziness. Emergency medical technicians arrived nine minutes later, confirmed a palpable carotid pulse with agonal-appearing spontaneous respirations at 10 breaths per minute, applied a rigid cervical collar, log-rolled him onto a long spine board, obtained a capillary glucose of 118 mg/dL, and inserted a 16-gauge peripheral IV in the left antecubital fossa that was flushed with 5 mL of normal saline only. No oxygen, crystalloid bolus, dextrose, naloxone, benzodiazepine, opioid, paralytic, antiarrhythmic, vasopressor, or hyperosmolar agent was administered in the field. Ground transport of nine minutes brought him to the resuscitation bay at 07:46. Upon arrival he lies motionless on the backboard; both lids are naturally parted, and dark irides drift slowly without fixing on faces or objects. Pupils measure 3 mm bilaterally, are round, and constrict promptly to direct and consensual light; corneal reflexes are present. Vital signs obtained concurrently with the first in-hospital neurologic survey—before any medications—are blood pressure 148/82 mm Hg in the right brachial artery, heart rate 94 beats per minute with an irregularly irregular rhythm on the monitor, respiratory rate 12 per minute with shallow abdominal expansion, oxygen saturation 96 % while breathing ambient air, and rectal temperature 36.6 °C. The airway is clear of secretions, dentition is intact, uvula midline, and a gentle sweep with a Yankauer catheter provokes a brisk gag followed by a single cough. Throughout repeated verbal prompts delivered at escalating volume directly beside each ear, he neither utters recognizable words nor produces groan, moan, or other vocalization; jaw movement is absent except for the aforementioned gag. Cranial nerve examination otherwise shows symmetric nasolabial folds at rest and a midline tongue when the mandible is passively opened. Upper and lower limbs rest flaccidly along the torso. When a firm trapezius squeeze is applied on the right, the ipsilateral shoulder elevates, elbow flexes, and his hand travels toward the examiner’s grasp, attempting to dislodge it; an identical purposeful reach is elicited by nail-bed compression of the left index finger, and no hemiparesis is appreciated. There is no decorticate or decerebrate extension, and no generalized withdrawal pattern. Between stimuli he does not follow commands such as “show two fingers” or “wiggle your toes,” and spontaneous movement of extremities is absent. Muscle tone is otherwise decreased; deep tendon reflexes are 2 + at biceps, triceps, patellae, and Achilles, and plantar stimulation produces a flexor response bilaterally without clonus. Cardiovascular examination reveals variable intensity S1 and a soft systolic flow murmur at the apex consistent with known cardiomyopathy; peripheral pulses are 2 + and symmetric with capillary refill under two seconds. Lung fields are clear to auscultation with equal air entry and resonant percussion; no crepitus or paradoxical chest wall motion is present. Abdomen is flat, soft, and nontender with active bowel sounds; there is no distention or guarding. Pelvic ring is stable to gentle anteroposterior and lateral compression. Log-roll inspection exposes scattered ecchymoses over the thoracolumbar spine but no step-off or open wounds, and sacrococcygeal palpation is non-tender. Bilateral lower extremities show intact alignment without deformity; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are palpable. Skin is warm, non-diaphoretic, and free of petechiae or purpura; a 1.5 cm superficial laceration is noted along the lateral aspect of the left eyebrow, oozing minimal venous blood, and has not been irrigated or dressed. Point-of-care arterial blood gas on room air demonstrates pH 7.38, PaCO₂ 41 mm Hg, PaO₂ 88 mm Hg, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, and base excess −1 mEq/L. Portable anterior-posterior chest radiograph obtained within five minutes shows clear lung fields, normal mediastinal silhouette, and no rib fractures; supine pelvic film is unremarkable. Focused assessment with sonography for trauma reveals no pericardial or intraperitoneal fluid. Blood for complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation profile, serum ethanol, type and screen, high-sensitivity troponin, and urine toxicology has been sent but is not yet resulted. No sedative, analgesic, neuromuscular blocking agent, antihypertensive, or intravenous fluid beyond the pre-hospital saline flush has been given in the department, ensuring that the neurologic findings described—naturally open eyes, absence of vocalization, and purposeful reaching toward painful stimuli—represent the patient’s untreated baseline at presentation. Trauma surgery, neurosurgery, and neurocritical care have been paged; stat non-contrast CT of the head and cervical spine and CT angiography of the neck are being arranged, airway equipment for rapid sequence intubation is at bedside should his respiratory effort decline, and nursing staff have instituted fifteen-minute neurologic checks while preparation for potential reversal of anticoagulation proceeds pending imaging.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow Coma Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow Coma Scale sums the best eye-opening (1–4), verbal (1–5), and motor (1–6) responses. On the untreated admission examination:
• Eyes were open without stimulation: spontaneous opening, E4. Visual tracking is not required.
• No words or sounds: V1. The reflex gag and cough are not verbal responses.
• He reached toward the examiner's hand to remove the painful stimulus: localizes pain, M5. This is more purposeful than withdrawal, but he did not obey commands.
GCS = E4 + V1 + M5 = 10.
Final answer: 10
